subject: maths
title: Measuring: Length, Mass, Capacity and Temperature
seo_title: Year 2 Measuring Worksheets: Rulers, Scales, Jugs and Thermometers (Free, with Answers)
standard_text: Choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure length/height in any direction (m/cm); mass (kg/g); temperature (°C); capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit, using rulers, scales, thermometers and measuring vessels; compare and order lengths, mass, volume/capacity and record the results using >, < and =.
meta_desc: Free Year 2 maths worksheets on measuring: lengths in cm with a ruler, mass in kg and g on scales, capacity in ml and litres in jugs, temperature in °C on a thermometer, choosing sensible units and comparing with <, > and =. 100 questions with an answer key, matched to the National Curriculum.
key_big: Start at 0, find what each mark is worth, and always check the unit.
key_sub: A pencil is about 15 cm, not 15 m. 5 kg is heavier than 50 g, because a kilogram is much heavier than a gram.
body_html:
What we measure

We measure with units. Each kind of measure has its own units and its own tool.

MeasureUnitsTool
Length and height (how long or tall)centimetres (cm), metres (m)ruler, metre stick
Mass (how heavy)grams (g), kilograms (kg)weighing scale
Capacity (how much it holds)millilitres (ml), litresmeasuring jug
Temperature (how hot or cold)degrees Celsius (°C)thermometer

Use small units for small things and big units for big things. A pencil is about 15 cm long. A door is about 2 m tall.

Measure with a ruler

Put one end of the object on 0, not on 1 and not on the edge of the ruler. Read the number at the other end.

If the object does not start at 0, count the spaces from the start to the end.

Read a scale, a jug or a thermometer

Not every mark has a number. First find what each mark is worth. Look at how the numbers go up, and count the spaces between them. Then count on from the number before.

Compare and order

Use < (less than), > (more than) and = (equal to). The open side faces the bigger amount. Check the units as well as the numbers.

Which is longer?

2 m or 90 cm?

1 m = 100 cm, so 2 m = 200 cm. 200 cm is more than 90 cm.

Answer: 2 m > 90 cm

Which is heavier?

5 kg or 50 g?

A kilogram is much heavier than a gram. 5 kg is more, even though 5 is less than 50.

Answer: 5 kg > 50 g

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Starting the ruler at 1 or at the edgeStart at 0, or count the spaces from the start
Counting every mark on a scale as 1Work out what each mark is worth first
Reading the next number on the scaleCount on from the number before the needle
Saying a pencil is 15 m longSmall things are measured in cm, big things in m
Saying 50 g is more than 5 kgLook at the units: 1 kg = 1,000 g

faq.q: What measuring do Year 2 children learn?
faq.a: Year 2 pupils measure length and height in cm and m, mass in kg and g, capacity in litres and ml, and temperature in °C. They use rulers, scales, jugs and thermometers, and compare with <, > and =.

faq.q: How do you teach a Year 2 child to use a ruler?
faq.a: Show them how to put one end of the object on 0, not on 1 or the edge of the ruler. Then read the number at the other end and say the unit, such as 6 cm.

faq.q: How do you read a scale when not every mark has a number?
faq.a: Look at how the numbers go up and count the spaces between two numbers to find what each mark is worth. Then count on from the number before the needle or the water line.

faq.q: Do Year 2 children need to know that 1 m = 100 cm?
faq.a: Year 2 pupils choose the right unit and compare measures. Knowing that 1 m = 100 cm and 1 kg = 1,000 g helps them see that 2 m is longer than 90 cm.

sets.title: Measure length with a ruler in cm

items.q: Which unit would you use to measure the length of a pencil?
items.e: A pencil is short. It fits on a ruler, so use centimetres.

items.q: Which unit would you use to measure the length of the school hall?
items.e: The hall is long. Use metres for long things.

items.q: Which unit would you use to measure how tall a tree is?
items.e: A tree is tall. Use metres. Kilograms and litres do not measure length.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: The pencil starts at 0 and ends at 6. So it is 6 cm long. Count the spaces, not the numbers.

items.q: How long is the rubber?
items.e: The rubber starts at 0 and ends at 4. So it is 4 cm long. Count the spaces, not the numbers.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: The pencil starts at 2, not at 0. Count the spaces from 2 to 8: there are 6. Or work it out: 8 − 2 = 6. So it is 6 cm long.

items.q: How long is the rubber?
items.e: The rubber starts at 1, not at 0. Count the spaces from 1 to 5: there are 4. Or work it out: 5 − 1 = 4. So it is 4 cm long.

items.q: How long is the crayon?
items.e: The crayon starts at 3, not at 0. Count the spaces from 3 to 10: there are 7. Or work it out: 10 − 3 = 7. So it is 7 cm long.

items.q: How long is the ribbon?
items.e: The ribbon starts at 2, not at 0. Count the spaces from 2 to 11: there are 9. Or work it out: 11 − 2 = 9. So it is 9 cm long.

items.q: How long is the crayon?
items.e: The crayon starts at 4, not at 0. Count the spaces from 4 to 9: there are 5. Or work it out: 9 − 4 = 5. So it is 5 cm long.

items.q: How long is the pencil?
items.e: The pencil starts at 1, not at 0. Count the spaces from 1 to 9: there are 8. Or work it out: 9 − 1 = 8. So it is 8 cm long.

items.q: Harry puts one end of his pencil on 1, not on 0. The other end is on 8. How long is the pencil?
items.e: The pencil starts at 1, so 8 is not the answer. 8 − 1 = 7. The pencil is 7 cm long.

sets.title: Read scales: mass in kg and g

items.q: Which unit would you use to find the mass of a bag of potatoes?
items.e: Mass is how heavy something is. We measure mass in kilograms (kg) or grams (g).

items.q: What is the best estimate for the mass of an apple?
items.e: An apple is light. It is about 100 grams. 100 kg is heavier than a grown-up.

items.q: What is the best estimate for the mass of a bag of sugar?
items.e: A bag of sugar is about 1 kilogram. 1 g is about as heavy as a paper clip.

items.q: What is the best estimate for the mass of a Year 2 child?
items.e: A Year 2 child is about 20 kilograms. 20 g is lighter than a bar of chocolate.

items.q: The scale shows a bag of potatoes. What is the mass?
items.e: Every mark has a number. The needle is right on 3. So it is 3 kg.

items.q: The scale shows a bag of pasta. What is the mass?

items.q: The scale shows a pumpkin. What is the mass?

items.q: The scale shows a bag of dog food. What is the mass?

items.q: The scale shows a block of cheese. What is the mass?

items.q: The scale shows a bag of rice. What is the mass?

items.q: The scale shows a bunch of bananas. What is the mass?

The numbers go up in 5s. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 1 kg. Count on from 10: 11, 12. So it is 12 kg.

items.q: The scale shows a big bag of sand. What is the mass?
items.e: The numbers go up in 5s. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 1 kg. Count on from 15: 16, 17, 18. So it is 18 kg.

items.q: The scale shows a parcel. Mum puts a 2 kg bag on the scale too. What will the scale show now?
items.e: The needle is at 6 kg. Mum adds 2 kg, so add: 6 + 2 = 8 kg.

items.q: The scale shows some flour. How much more flour is needed to make 500 g?
items.e: The needle is at 300 g. Count on from 300 to 500: 400, 500. That is 200 g more.

sets.title: Read jugs: capacity in ml and litres

items.q: Which unit would you use to measure the water in a bath?
items.e: A bath holds a lot of water. We measure lots of water in litres.

items.q: Which unit would you use to measure medicine on a spoon?
items.e: A spoon holds only a little. We measure a little water in millilitres (ml).

items.q: What is the best estimate for how much a cup holds?
items.e: A cup holds about 200 millilitres. 200 litres would fill a bath.

items.q: What is the best estimate for how much a bucket holds?
items.e: A bucket holds about 10 litres. 10 ml is only two teaspoons.

items.q: What is the best estimate for how much a teaspoon holds?
items.e: A teaspoon holds only a little, about 5 millilitres.

items.q: What do we use to measure temperature?
items.e: A thermometer measures how hot or cold something is. Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (°C).

items.q: What is the best estimate for the temperature in a classroom?
items.e: A classroom is warm, but not hot. It is about 20 °C.

items.q: What is the best estimate for the temperature outside on a hot summer day in the UK?
items.e: A hot day in the UK is about 25 °C. 5 °C is cold, and 100 °C is as hot as boiling water.

items.q: What is the best estimate for the temperature outside on a snowy day?
items.e: Snow needs it to be very cold. Water freezes at 0 °C, so a snowy day is about 2 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is outside on a cold morning. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 5s. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 1 °C. Count on from 5: 6, 7. So it is 7 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is in the garden. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 5s. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 1 °C. Count on from 10: 11, 12, 13. So it is 13 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is in the school hall. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 5s. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 1 °C. Count on from 15: 16, 17, 18. So it is 18 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is in the playground. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 10s. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 5 °C. Count on from 10: 15. So it is 15 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is outside on a sunny day. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 10s. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 5 °C. Count on from 20: 25. So it is 25 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is in a greenhouse in summer. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 10s. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 5 °C. Count on from 30: 35. So it is 35 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is in the park in spring. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 10s. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 2 °C. Count on from 10: 12, 14. So it is 14 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is on the beach. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 10s. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 2 °C. Count on from 20: 22, 24, 26. So it is 26 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is in a hot car. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 10s. There are 5 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 2 °C. Count on from 30: 32. So it is 32 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is in a cup of tea. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 20s. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 10 °C. Count on from 60: 70. So it is 70 °C.

items.q: This thermometer is in water from the kettle. What temperature does it show?
items.e: The numbers go up in 20s. There are 2 spaces between two numbers, so each mark is 10 °C. Count on from 80: 90. So it is 90 °C.

items.q: On Monday it was 14 °C. On Tuesday it was 9 °C. Which is true?
items.e: 14 is more than 9, so Monday was warmer. 14 °C > 9 °C. The open side of > faces the bigger number.

items.q: Which temperature is the coldest?
items.e: The coldest temperature is the smallest number. 2 is smaller than 12, 20 and 21.

items.q: It gets 5 degrees warmer. What will the temperature be?
items.e: The thermometer shows 12 °C. Warmer means add: 12 + 5 = 17 °C.

items.q: It gets 10 degrees warmer. What will the temperature be?
items.e: Each mark is 5 °C, so it shows 30 °C. Warmer means add: 30 + 10 = 40 °C.

items.q: At night it gets 6 degrees colder. What will the temperature be?
items.e: The thermometer shows 20 °C. Colder means take away: 20 − 6 = 14 °C.

sets.title: Compare measures and solve word problems

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: Look at the tens. 4 tens is less than 5 tens, so 45 cm < 54 cm.

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: A metre stick has 100 centimetres on it. So 1 m = 100 cm.

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: 1 m = 100 cm, so 2 m = 200 cm. 200 cm is more than 90 cm. Do not just compare 2 and 90.

items.q: Which is true?
items.e: A kilogram is much heavier than a gram: 1 kg = 1,000 g. So 5 kg is more than 50 g, even though 5 is less than 50.

items.q: Which holds the most?
items.e: 1 litre = 1,000 ml. That is more than 500 ml. Look at the units, not just the numbers.

items.q: Which list goes from the shortest to the longest?
items.e: 9 is the smallest number and 21 is the biggest. So the order is 9 cm, 12 cm, 21 cm.

items.q: Which list goes from the lightest to the heaviest?
items.e: 5 is the smallest number and 50 is the biggest. So the order is 5 kg, 15 kg, 50 kg.

items.q: About how long is a pencil?
items.e: A pencil fits on a ruler, so it is about 15 cm. 15 m is longer than a classroom!

items.q: About how tall is a door?
items.e: A door is taller than a grown-up, so it is about 2 m. 2 cm is shorter than your finger.

items.q: Lily has 45 cm of ribbon. She cuts off 20 cm. How much ribbon is left?
items.e: Cutting off means take away: 45 − 20 = 25 cm.

items.q: Evie has two pieces of string. One is 23 cm long. The other is 34 cm long. How much string is there altogether?
items.e: Altogether means add: 23 + 34 = 57 cm.

items.q: A sunflower is 60 cm tall. It grows 25 cm more. How tall is it now?
items.e: It grows, so add: 60 + 25 = 85 cm.

items.q: Leo builds a tower 48 cm tall. Charlie builds a tower 30 cm tall. How much taller is Leo’s tower?
items.e: How much taller means find the difference: 48 − 30 = 18 cm.

items.q: A cat weighs 4 kg. A dog weighs 12 kg. How much heavier is the dog?
items.e: Find the difference: 12 − 4 = 8 kg.

items.q: Ruby makes biscuits. She uses 50 g of butter and 40 g of sugar. How much is that altogether?
items.e: Altogether means add: 50 + 40 = 90 g.

items.q: Noah has a 500 ml bottle of water. He drinks 200 ml at lunchtime. How much water is left?
items.e: Drinks means take away: 500 − 200 = 300 ml.

items.q: A bucket holds 5 litres. How much water do 4 buckets hold?
items.e: 4 lots of 5 litres: 5, 10, 15, 20. So 4 × 5 = 20 litres.

items.q: George fills a 10 litre paddling pool with a 2 litre jug. How many jugs of water does he need?
items.e: How many 2s make 10? Count in 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. That is 5 jugs. 10 ÷ 2 = 5.

items.q: In the morning it was 8 °C. At lunchtime it was 15 °C. How many degrees warmer was it at lunchtime?
items.e: Find the difference. Count on from 8 to 15: 8 to 10 is 2, 10 to 15 is 5. 2 + 5 = 7 °C.

items.q: In the afternoon it was 21 °C. In the evening it was 6 degrees colder. What was the temperature in the evening?
items.e: Colder means take away: 21 − 6 = 15 °C.
